hints: Think about what would make a vaccine stop working over time, look at options C and D and ask yourself what mutation does to the shape of viral antigens.
For eradication to be possible, the virus must have nowhere to hide between outbreaks, so think about animal hosts in option A and staying hidden in the body in option B.
walkthrough:
**What does eradication need?**

To wipe out a disease completely, a vaccine must keep working everywhere, and the virus must have nowhere to hide.

That means stable antigens, only human hosts, and no long-term latency.

**Check smallpox biology**

Smallpox virus infected only humans, so there was no animal reservoir to restart infection.

It also caused an acute infection that was either cleared by immunity or killed the host, it did not stay dormant to reactivate later like chickenpox does.

**Why stability mattered**

Most importantly, the smallpox virus was genetically stable.

Its surface antigens did not change much, so one vaccine gave long-lasting protection worldwide and the virus could not escape immunity by mutation.

options.A: False, smallpox infected only humans. Having no animal reservoir made it easier, not harder, to break the transmission cycle.
options.B: False, smallpox did not remain latent in the body. This lack of hiding made eradication possible, unlike viruses that reactivate later.
options.C: Correct, the virus was antigenically stable with very little mutation, so the same vaccine remained effective everywhere.
options.D: False, this is the opposite of the truth. An unstable, highly mutating virus like influenza would quickly escape vaccine immunity.
